Eggs of the Raggiana bird-of-paradise, incubated in the humid lowland forests of New Guinea at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], typically hatch after an incubation period of 20 days [ab = 20 days]. The freshly hatched altricial nestlings emerge with a remarkably low body mass; measurements indicate a mean weight at birth of 12.1 grams [Wwb = 12.1 grams], a value calculated from the egg dimensions of 36.4 millimeters in length and 25.2 millimeters in width. This initial mass is relatively modest even among passerines of comparable adult size, reflecting the energetically constrained conditions of yolk-dependent development. Shortly after hatching, the nestling enters the brooded chick stage, requiring constant parental provisioning. The rate of growth during this early phase is substantial, as the nestling must more than double its mass repeatedly before reaching independence. Parental investment is consequently high, with both males and females contributing to feeding the developing chick.

Under the thermal regime characteristic of this species' active metabolic period, which centers around 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the developmental trajectory of the nestling proceeds through several well-defined milestones. The first of these is fledging, the achievement of sustained flight, which takes place at 18.5 days since birth [tx = 18.5 days since birth] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This early fledging age is advantageous in a predator-rich environment, allowing the young bird to escape terrestrial threats. Following fledging, the juvenile bird continues to be dependent on the parents for several weeks as its foraging skills improve. The transition from a fully dependent nestling to a nutritionally independent juvenile is a critical period marked by high mortality. Field studies indicate that the survival rate through this phase is relatively low, a pattern common among many tropical passerines that invest heavily in a small number of offspring. The relatively rapid fledging age may be an adaptation to minimize the time spent in the vulnerable nest site.

Under the typical thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], sexual maturation in the Raggiana bird-of-paradise is a protracted process, especially for males, who require several years to develop the elaborate ornamental plumage necessary for successful lekking. The age at puberty, defined as the onset of gonad maturation, is estimated at 84 days since birth [tp = 84 days since birth] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. However, this physiological milestone by no means coincides with the initiation of reproductive activity; actual breeding is deferred considerably. The time since birth at first brood, representing the age at which a female produces her first successful clutch, is 1.8 years since birth [tR = 1.8 years since birth] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This significant delay between achieving puberty and first reproduction is characteristic of many bird-of-paradise species. It reflects the time required for males to establish a territory and attain their full adult plumage, and for females to accumulate sufficient resources for egg production. Young males often act as satellite individuals at leks before they are capable of securing mating opportunities.

Under the thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], adult body mass exhibits a striking degree of sexual dimorphism in this species, as is typical of lekking polygynous birds. The ultimate wet weight for females stabilizes around 185 grams [Wwi = around 185 grams], while males attain a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 272 grams [Wwi = 272 grams]. This disparity in mass is not solely attributable to the larger skeletal frame of the male; a considerable portion of the difference is accounted for by the elongated flank feathers, the rich crimson and maroon plumes used in intricate courtship displays. When considering reproductive output, females produce a single brood per year [F_R_i = a single brood per year], laying a clutch of one egg [N_R_i = a clutch of one egg] during each breeding season. This low reproductive rate is balanced by a relatively high adult survival rate and a maximum recorded lifespan of 33 years [am = 33 years] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], which is a significant longevity for a passerine of this body size. The combination of delayed maturation, low fecundity, and long life defines a slow life-history strategy.

The energetic demands of sustaining such an extended life cycle, even at rest, are not trivial. Basal metabolic rate measurements conducted on resting adults under a thermoneutral ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] recorded an oxygen consumption of 337.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 337.5 milliliters per hour]. This value represents the maximum resting metabolic rate for the species and reflects the high cost of maintaining a large, active brain and a sophisticated neuromuscular system necessary for the complex aerial displays. The 185 gram females, being considerably smaller, likely have a higher mass-specific metabolic rate than their larger male counterparts, though this has not been directly measured. The relatively large clutch size in terms of energy investment—a single, nutritionally rich egg—is consistent with a strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity. Despite the high per-offspring investment, the annual reproductive rate is constrained to a single young per brood [N_R_i = single young per brood] per female, a value far below what would be predicted for a bird of this body mass, emphasizing the extreme end of the slow life-history continuum among passerines.
